subject: Query: Example code for BDA section 22.4 or Exercise 22.2?

messages.author: ebac19664dad3407
messages.subject: Query: Example code for BDA section 22.4 or Exercise 22.2?
parts:
I am trying to analyze the ages of a bunch of zircon crystals using a Gaussian mixture model with an unspecified number of components (my gut-feeling prior is around 3 or so). I have several sets of about 100 age measurements and I want to analyze each set.

The problem is almost identical to the galaxy and acidity examples in section 22.4 of BDA (3rd ed.), or exercise 2(d) for chapter 22: I have a one-dimensional vector of about age measurements ranging from 40 to 300 kiloyears (apart from age, there is nothing to distinguish one zircon from another for the purposes of this analysis) and I want to identify clusters to help some geologist colleagues unscramble a puzzle about magma dynamics. The data isn't clearly multimodal, but it has hints of being bimodal (although that could also be noise), as well as being highly skewed with a long tail.

I can analyze the data using the EM algorithm with Fraley and Raferty's mclust R package, but I'm interested in comparing that approach to MCMC (following the discussion on pp. 523-4 of BDA and at the beginning of 22.4) and I am trying to figure out whether it's better to try this in JAGS or Stan.

So I'm wondering whether anyone has implemented anything like the galaxy and acidity examples in Stan so I can adapt them to my problem. (Of course, maybe Stan isn't the right tool for the job, since there are discrete Dirichlet-distributed parameters pi_h in the way Gelman et al. formulate the problem in 22.4, in which case a Gibbs sampler, such as JAGS, might be the better choice.)

If I can model this with Stan, I will be happy to post the model and example data, both to help others and to benefit from the wisdom of comments from folks here, who know lots more than I do.

parts: The problem is almost identical to the galaxy and acidity examples in section 22.4 of BDA (3rd ed.), or exercise 2(d) for chapter 22: I have a one-dimensional vector of about age measurements ranging from 40 to 300 kiloyears (apart from age, there is nothing to distinguish one zircon from another for the purposes of this analysis) and I want to identify clusters to help some geologist colleagues unscramble a puzzle about magma dynamics. The data isn't clearly multimodal, but it has hints of being bimodal (although that could also be noise), as well as being highly skewed with a long tail.

Note that the if the clusters are not well separated and if the data generating process is not mixture of Gaussians (more skewed, longer tails) you will have problems in interpretation as you need more Gaussians to describe non-Gaussian components. This is nicely illustrated in http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs11222-012-9351-7 (see, e.g., Galaxy data in Fig 5).

Aki

parts:
On Mar 23, 2014, at 7:42 PM, Jonathan Gilligan <jonathan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I am trying to analyze the ages of a bunch of zircon crystals using a Gaussian mixture model with an unspecified number of components (my gut-feeling prior is around 3 or so). I have several sets of about 100 age measurements and I want to analyze each set.
>
> The problem is almost identical to the galaxy and acidity examples in section 22.4 of BDA (3rd ed.), or exercise 2(d) for chapter 22: I have a one-dimensional vector of about age measurements ranging from 40 to 300 kiloyears (apart from age, there is nothing to distinguish one zircon from another for the purposes of this analysis) and I want to identify clusters to help some geologist colleagues unscramble a puzzle about magma dynamics. The data isn't clearly multimodal, but it has hints of being bimodal (although that could also be noise), as well as being highly skewed with a long tail.
>
> I can analyze the data using the EM algorithm with Fraley and Raferty's mclust R package, but I'm interested in comparing that approach to MCMC (following the discussion on pp. 523-4 of BDA and at the beginning of 22.4) and I am trying to figure out whether it's better to try this in JAGS or Stan.

This is the kind of problem that Stan's good at.

It's a bit trickier to model because you have to marginalize out the
discrete cluster "responsibility" parameter. The upside is that you
get faster mixing in the sampler without the discrete parameter.

If you do comparisons with JAGS or any other software, we'd love to hear about
them.

>
> So I'm wondering whether anyone has implemented anything like the galaxy and acidity examples in Stan so I can adapt them to my problem.

Chapter 13 of the Stan manual explains mixture modeling with examples
you could follow to do this.

There are also examples of how to formulate K-means clustering as
a Gaussian mixture.

You have a wide range of choices on the prior and how the clusters
are modeled (fixed covariance matrix or estimated).

If your data are just one-dimensional (really just ages and no
other predictors?) then the model's particularly simple as you can
do it all with regular normals rather than multivariate ones.

> (Of course, maybe Stan isn't the right tool for the job, since there are discrete Dirichlet-distributed parameters pi_h in the way Gelman et al. formulate the problem in 22.4, in which case a Gibbs sampler, such as JAGS, might be the better choice.)

pi ~ dirichlet(ones);

is no problem in Stan. You declare pi as a simplex and ones as a
vector of 1. In fact, this is basically a no-op in Stan because
dirichlet(1...1) is the identity and that's the default prior if
one isn't specified.

It's the discrete parameters that you sample

z[i] ~ discrete(pi);

that need to be marginalized out.

The Stan code essentially directly codes the initial mixture-model
formula (22.1) without creating an intermediate discrete parameter.

>
> If I can model this with Stan, I will be happy to post the model and example data, both to help others and to benefit from the wisdom of comments from folks here, who know lots more than I do.

Thanks. We always like seeing concrete models.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Query: Example code for BDA section 22.4 or Exercise 22.2?
parts:
Thanks, Bob and Aki for your comments and suggestions.

Aki's caution about poorly separated components and possibly non-Gaussian distributions is a real concern for me, so I'll look at the paper you suggest, which looks very relevant from the abstract. Some quick and dirty analysis with other some canned software shows this in a big way: mclust finds two clusters with EM, but Arnošt Komárek's mixAK (a reversible-jump MCMC) tends to find far more clusters than I find plausible and dramatically overfits the data if I run it with its default parameters. This is why I need to understand clearly what I am doing from the ground up and why I want to compare different approaches.

Bob, your assurance that this is a problem Stan's good at is encouraging. I wanted to ask before I devoted a bunch of time to it. Now I'm ready to get to work. It really is a one-dimensional problem with no predictors. I'm kind of slow so I will probably disappear off this thread for some time while I work on instantiating a model in stan and then I will come back when I have something to share or if I run into a roadblock.

Thanks much to both of you!
